title: Lena and the Compass
premise: In 1848, on the eve of revolution in a river city under an aging empire, Rosalind Hartwell cuts typefaces by day in her father's print shop and keeps her head down. When a wounded stranger named Tomas arrives carrying a letter written in the unmistakable hand of her brother Emil—declared dead two years ago at the frontier—Rosalind is pulled into a smuggling network that moves people, not just pamphlets, across the frozen river. As the secret police close in and her father's loyalty to the crown collides with her own, Rosalind discovers the network has one last berth on the final crossing before the ice breaks: room for exactly one person. In the end she gives the berth to her father, who has quietly been the network's silent financier all along, and stays behind with Tomas to face the soldiers—surviving not by fleeing, but by printing the truth as the city rises.
about_author: A. M. Halloran is the pen name of a former typesetter's apprentice who spent a decade restoring nineteenth-century letterpress equipment before turning to fiction. Halloran writes historical novels about ordinary hands caught in extraordinary machinery of history.

chapters.title: The Weight of Lead
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. We meet the Hartwell print shop: her father Alois cutting matrices, her mother dead three winters, the rhythm of honest work under censorship laws. Rosalind prides herself on being unremarkable. Emotional beat: quiet competence masking grief, establishing what 'invisible' costs her.

chapters.title: A Stranger at the Loading Door
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. A bleeding man collapses against the loading door at closing time, clutching a satchel. He begs for ink and paper, nothing else. She hides him before the night watch passes. Emotional beat: fear warring with curiosity—the first crack in her invisibility.

chapters.title: Handwriting of the Dead
chapters.summary: Tomas's POV. Delirious, he shows Rosalind the letter he carries: instructions in Emil Hartwell's hand, dated four months ago. Rosalind recognizes every ligature; she taught him half of them. Emotional beat: vertigo and hope—her brother lives, and everything she believed about his death is a lie.

chapters.title: What Father Keeps Locked
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. She searches the shop while Alois dines with the magistrate and finds a ledger of payments to names she doesn't know—and a second key to the cellar. Emotional beat: dawning suspicion that her father's respectability is a performance, and she was cast in it without consent.

chapters.title: The Network of Small Hands
chapters.summary: Tomas's POV. Recovering, Tomas explains the route: printers who move fugitives south under bales of waste paper, funded by an anonymous benefactor he knows only as 'the Cutter.' Emotional beat: reluctant trust between strangers bound by one impossible signature.

chapters.title: Emil, Alive and Elsewhere
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. The letter reveals Emil deserted the imperial army and now guides crossings from the far bank—but the letter also warns that someone inside the city network talks. Emotional beat: joy curdling into dread; her brother needs her, and so does the man bleeding in her cellar.

chapters.title: The Magistrate's Invitation
chapters.summary: Alois's POV. Magistrate Voss, an old friend, hints that the crown suspects the print quarter and offers Alois protection—in exchange for names. Alois deflects, but we see his fear is not for himself. Emotional beat: duty straining against a loyalty he cannot speak aloud.

chapters.title: Lessons in Disguise
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. She teaches Tomas to set type so he can pass as a journeyman; their hands keep meeting over the composing stick. Emotional beat: tenderness growing in stolen hours, guilt shadowing it because every hour spent flirting is an hour the traitor works.

chapters.title: The Raid on Binder's Lane
chapters.summary: Tomas's POV. Soldiers raid a safehouse two streets over; two couriers are taken. Tomas realizes the arrests began only after he entered the city—he may have been followed. Emotional beat: shame and urgency; his arrival may be the noose tightening around everyone.

chapters.title: Father's Ledger, Opened
chapters.summary: Rosalind confronts Alois with the ledger. He confesses: he is 'the Cutter,' funding the crossings since Emil's supposed death, hiding his treason inside impeccable loyalty. Emotional beat: fury dissolving into awe—her dull, careful father braver than she ever imagined.

chapters.title: Voss's Quiet Question
chapters.summary: Alois's POV. Voss visits the shop, runs a finger over a fresh matrix, and mentions a stranger seen near the loading door. Alois lies smoothly and hates how easily it comes. Emotional beat: the terrible fluency of betrayal; love measured now in lies told well.

chapters.title: The Informer's Face
chapters.summary: Tomas's POV. Cross-referencing arrest dates with delivery schedules, Tomas identifies the leak: young Petra, the errand girl who adores Rosalind, coerced by threats to her family. Emotional beat: sickening compassion—no villain here, only another person paying survival's price.

chapters.title: Ice groaning on the River
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. The thaw approaches; the final crossing must happen within days or not until autumn. Emil sends word: one berth, one passenger, no exceptions. Emotional beat: hope sharpened into arithmetic—who goes, who stays, who decides.

chapters.title: Petra's Confession
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. Petra breaks down and confesses everything, begging forgiveness. Rosalind must choose: turn her out to save the network, or protect her and risk them all. Emotional beat: mercy as a gamble; loyalty tested against truth's cold demands.

chapters.title: A False Manifest
chapters.summary: Tomas's POV. To buy time, they feed Voss a forged shipping manifest through Petra, turning the informer into a double agent. It works—for now. Emotional beat: exhilaration and dread entwined; deception has become their native language.

chapters.title: The Night Before the Crossing
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. Preparations in the cellar: papers forged on the shop's own press, Tomas and Rosalind admitting their love in whispers neither can promise to honor. Emotional beat: love fully acknowledged precisely when it may be most useless.

chapters.title: Whose Name Goes in the Book
chapters.summary: Alois's POV. The berth question detonates: Rosalind insists Emil should come home; Alois argues the network needs its guide alive; Tomas volunteers himself. Alois secretly writes his own name in the crossing book. Emotional beat: each claiming sacrifice as a form of love.

chapters.title: The Last Berth
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. She discovers her father's name on the manifest and understands: he means to take her place, believing the shop—and she—will be safer with him gone. She tears the page out and writes his name back in anyway, choosing him over Emil. Emotional beat: the book's central wound—love expressed as an unbearable choice.

chapters.title: The Ice Breaks
chapters.summary: Tomas's POV. The crossing at dawn: Alois departs downriver as the ice cracks like cannon fire, and Voss's men arrive at the shop minutes too late—but not empty-handed; they found Petra's real confession hidden in the loft. Emotional beat: triumph and trap springing in the same breath.

chapters.title: Soldiers in the Shop
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. Arrested and interrogated by Voss, Rosalind refuses to give a single name, reciting instead the shop's legitimate orders until Voss loses patience. Tomas surrenders himself to split the blame. Emotional beat: stillness under pressure; she has stopped surviving invisibly and started surviving loudly.

chapters.title: The Press Runs at Midnight
chapters.summary: Multiple POVs converging. With the magistrates distracted by the crossing scandal, the remaining network seizes the shop's press and prints ten thousand broadsheets naming Voss's abuses; the city wakes to paper on every door. Rosalind, released for lack of evidence, sets the final line herself. Emotional beat: catharsis—the typeface cutter's daughter becomes the author of the uprising's voice.

chapters.title: Letters Across the Water
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV, epilogue. Autumn: letters arrive from Alois in exile, in Emil's hand at last, and in Tomas's—from the next town over, where he waits. The shop reopens under new management: hers. Emotional beat: bittersweet resolution—she lost her father's daily presence and gained a life built on truth; the compass was never the river, but the people worth steering for.
